analysis.one_liner: ICICI Bank is India's second-largest private-sector bank, lending to retail and corporate customers and taking deposits, with insurance and asset-management arms held through subsidiaries.
analysis.whats_happening: Q2 FY27 (July-Sept 2026) results were announced on 17 October 2026, just three days before this report. Standalone net profit rose 20.1% year-on-year to ₹14,843 crore and NII grew 17.7% to ₹25,339 crore, but net interest margin slipped to 4.18% from 4.36% in the June quarter. Headline loan growth of 30% included a large FCNR(B)-linked overseas lending book; stripped of that, growth was 24.1%.
analysis.plain_terms: Profit and lending both grew fast this quarter, and bad loans kept shrinking, which sounds unambiguously good. The catch is that margins - the spread the bank earns on its loans - are narrowing, and a chunk of the loan growth came from a foreign-currency deposit-backed book rather than core domestic lending. So the bank is growing, but partly by taking on business that earns it less per rupee lent, which is a different, less durable kind of growth than it looks like at first glance.
analysis.quarters: NIM has declined three quarters running: 4.30% (Sep 2025) to 4.36% (Jun 2026) to 4.18% (Sep 2026), management attributing this to a growing share of lower-margin overseas lending and a shift toward term deposits. Standalone PAT grew 20.1% YoY while consolidated PAT (reported separately at ₹16,333 crore) grew 22.3% - these are not directly comparable bases and should not be averaged. Management guided to normalised credit costs of up to 50bps once corporate recoveries, FCNR-related standard-asset provisions and seasonal agri provisions are excluded.
analysis.performance_read: The stock closed at ₹1,381 on 19 October 2026, just 5.7% below its July 2025 peak of ₹1,464.85 - this is a mild pullback, not a crash. Over 1 year it is roughly flat (+0.17%) but that beat the Nifty's -11.43% and peer HDFC Bank's -27.84%, so the 'outperformance' reflects a weak market and weak peer rather than a strong rally. Over 5 years ICICI is up 92.08% against the Nifty's 24.27% and HDFC Bank's -9.89%; HDFC Bank's weak long-run number is partly distorted by the dilutive July 2023 reverse merger with HDFC Ltd, which added shares and depressed per-share metrics, so the gap somewhat overstates ICICI's edge. ICICI's own 2014 and 2017 stock splits are already reflected in standard adjusted price series and need no further adjustment.
analysis.valuation_read: P/E estimates across sources range from about 17x to 20x (TTM readings vary by data provider) and P/B is roughly 2.6x, both well above the banking-sector medians (~15.5x and ~1.35x respectively). It is expensive because ROE (16.4%) and asset quality (GNPA 1.20%, NNPA 0.30%) are well above sector medians and have been improving - the market is paying for a demonstrated quality premium, not a cheap entry point. Whether that premium is justified depends on whether the current NIM compression is temporary or structural; on the numbers alone, this is not a cheap stock by any conventional multiple.
analysis.growth_read: This quarter's growth was volume-led, not margin-led: loans grew fast (30% headline, 24.1% adjusted for the FCNR book) while NIM fell from 4.36% to 4.18%. Domestic corporate loans grew 30.6% and business banking 33.8%, while retail/rural grew a more modest 14.8% and still makes up 51.6% of the book. Growing volume while margin shrinks is a weaker combination than growing both together, and is worth watching rather than celebrating at face value.
analysis.health_read: Asset quality is improving on paper: gross NPA fell to 1.20% (from 1.58% a year ago) and net NPA to 0.30%, with a provisioning coverage ratio of 75%. Capital is strong - CET1 at 16.01% and total capital adequacy at 16.68% - so there is no solvency concern. The live question is business risk, specifically whether margin compression from deposit-cost pressure and the overseas lending mix continues, not financial or balance-sheet risk.
analysis.ownership_read: ICICI Bank has no promoter group - its original promoter, ICICI Limited, was absorbed into the bank in a 2002 reverse merger - so promoter shareholding and pledging are both structurally 0%, which removes a governance risk present at many other listed companies. As of the most recent available filing (June 2026), FIIs held 49.82% and DIIs 42.31%, together over 92%, with retail holding about 7.4%. No subsequent (September 2026) shareholding pattern was located at the time of writing.
strengths: Standalone net profit up 20.1% YoY to ₹14,843 crore with NII up 17.7% to ₹25,339 crore (Q2 FY27)
Gross NPA improved to 1.20% and net NPA to 0.30%, both down from a year ago, with a 75% provisioning coverage ratio
Capital position strong: CET1 16.01%, total capital adequacy 16.68%
3-year and 5-year stock returns (51.75%/92.08%) well ahead of the Nifty (17.12%/24.27%)
watchpoints: NIM has fallen for three straight quarters, from 4.36% (Jun 2026) to 4.18% (Sep 2026)
Headline 30% loan growth is inflated by an FCNR(B)-linked overseas book; underlying growth is 24.1%
Standalone PAT growth (20.1%) and consolidated PAT growth (22.3%) are on different bases and should not be compared directly
Valuation (P/E ~17-20x, P/B ~2.6x) sits well above sector medians, leaving less room for error if margin pressure persists
analysis.one_thing: Whether NIM stabilises in H2 FY27 - continued compression from the FCNR book and deposit-cost pressure would undercut the case for the stock's premium valuation.
analysis.data_notes: Standalone PAT, NII and asset-quality figures cross-checked across five independent sources (Tribune, Zeebiz, BusinessToday, Newsdrum, TradingView) and were consistent. Consolidated PAT (₹16,333 crore, Business Standard) differs from the standalone figure and is flagged as non-comparable rather than averaged. P/E estimates varied by provider (16.8x to 20.47x); a range is given rather than a single invented number. Shareholding pattern reflects the June 2026 filing, the latest found; a September 2026 update could not be located and should be checked on Screener.
